newsitem.title: UK: Antimony unmoved by Chinese production cut - trade.
newsitem.headline: Antimony unmoved by Chinese production cut - trade.

text.p: European minor metal traders were initially cautious to news that major antimony producer China is to slash annual production by 20 percent, with opinions divided on the next price direction.
"It's wait and see at the moment...we have had similar moves by the Chinese in the past," one London trader said.

Others agreed, saying at present they were unprepared to move European antimony prices significantly but would closely eye further developments from a country that has around 50 percent of the world's known reserves.
"Its like a dripping tap which in all probability is likely to be turned off soon," another antimony trader said.
"My feelings this time round is that the Chinese will try to rigidly reinforce the proposed production cuts."

According to the China Daily newspaper the cuts would be implemented following rises in both domestic and international production, while prices for antimony have fallen over the last two years. "As a result, the state wants to limit production," it quoted the National Production Union for Antimony as saying.
Antimony is added to alloys to increase their strength and hardness and can be also utilised as a fire retardant and in some batteries.

Traders believe the announcement followed a meeting of the Chinese Antimony Producers Association held recently in Hunan. Several traders, referring to the proposed state intervention to curb production, remain unsure if the government could fully enforce the cuts.
"Most of the antimony mines and smelters are in the southern provinces of China," one noted.
He said, compared to the north, the south of China was more Westernised with many of the antimony facilities leased from the Chinese government by private enterprise.

"This should make any cuts hard to enforce," he said. Stock levels in China are hard to pin down, although traders believe they are at high levels, both inland and at exit ports, following the recent flooding which caused transport problems.

Antimony's next price move is likely to be dictated by consumer demand. "At the end of the day it's all down to how the consumers react," one trader said. Some believed they would now be tempted to cover at current levels in anticipation of a price spike, but others said they would also adopt a wait-and-see attitude.

Antimony is currently hovering around $2,500 a tonne, a significant psychological level, according to some traders. "A break of $2,500 could see a dive towards $2,200, but if consumers cover prices could easily bounce," one trader said.
The price had been as high as $5,900 in Novemeber 1994, but since the start of 1996 prices have fallen from levels of around $3,400. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 8075
